summary: AE + SE demo for Opal Analytics focused on worst-case session lengths (hundreds of thousands of tokens), very high TPS spikes, and streaming client backpressure/timeouts. Covered runtime strategies (KV/prefix caching, batching, tail latency controls), console observability, and Optimize recommendations. Security questions (KMS, audit logs, VPC) surfaced. Agreed to run a private trial + shared benchmarks.
topics: high TPS / burst behavior and autoscale
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-19
Start: 14:30 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Lena Morris (Redwood AE), Owen Patel (Redwood SE), Tara Nguyen (Redwood Product), Rajiv Menon (Opal CTO), Sofia Alvarez (Lead ML), Markus Li (Infra), Hannah Kim (PM)

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I m Lena, I'm the AE on this one, Owen is our SE, Tara is on product. How's it going at Opal?
[00:12] Rajiv: Good, thanks. Busy quarter, but we've got a new real-time use case — think multi-hour context windows for session analytics and sudden spikes from ingest. We wanted to see how Redwood handles the extreme tail.
[00:25] Owen: great context, Rajiv. Today we ll demo a few edge scenarios: very long contexts (we'll simulate ~200k to 500k token histories), high TPS bursts (thousands of requests per second for short windows), and streaming with clients that sometimes fall behind — backpressure and timeouts.
[00:41] Sofia: quick qual: we re currently running a mix of OpenAI hosted endpoints for shorter contexts, and on-prem for heavy workloads — looking to consolidate. Our infra constraints: must keep session data in our VPC for regulated customers.
[00:55] Lena: understood. We'll highlight Redwood Private and Dedicated options. Also show the console traces so you can see per-token latency and tail percentiles.
[01:10] Owen: ok jumping in — first slide: runtime behaviors. The big idea is: when sequence lengths blow up you need KV caching, prefix caching, and session pinning to avoid re-computing attention for the whole history. (audio glitch) sorry that was a little fuzzy, I said session pinning.
[01:30] [02:00] Owen: We're starting a live run — simulating 300k token history with a mixed request pattern. You might hear some overlapping audio as we speak to the runner process.
[02:15] Rajiv: quick Q — do you stream tokens from GPU or do you buffer full responses? In our current set up we often hit client-side timeouts because the frontend can't keep up.
[02:28] Owen: good question. Redwood streams tokens immediately; streaming path is async — tokens are emitted as soon as the runtime produces them. But when the client falls behind and doesn't read the TCP/window, you can see backpressure build up which can affect the worker's ability to schedule other tasks. We have a few mitigations: proactive throttling per-connection, socket-level timeouts, and streaming window quotas.
[02:50] Markus: when you say quota, is that enforced at the load balancer or the runtime? We have an L4 proxy in front and want to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[03:04] Owen: the enforcement is in the runtime + edge admission layer. We can signal the load balancer to shed or queue. There's also the option to configure a per-API streaming concurrency limit via the console.
[03:20] [04:00] Tara: jumping in with an Optimize note — for very long contexts we recommend a mix of prefix cache (for the common opening 50-100k tokens) and KV cache for recent tokens; plus a policy to truncate old metadata. That tends to reduce average token compute by 30-60% depending on your distribution.
[04:25] Sofia: 30-60% sounds optimistic, are those numbers from your public benchmarks? We need something more tailored.
[04:35] Tara: yes public numbers are general. We'll run a tailored benchmark using your token distribution if you share traces. That s why we're proposing the week-long private pilot.
[04:50] [05:15] Owen: demo is running — I m toggling a long-session flag that pins a session to a worker with a hot KV cache. You ll see the per-token latency on the console feed.
[05:30] [06:00] CONSOLE AUDIO NOTE: (screen share) Live dashboard shows streaming tokens and 99.9/99.99 tail. We're emitting logs every 30s.
[06:10] Rajiv: I m seeing a spike at 06:25 in the console — is that the moment you injected a burst?
[06:25] Owen: yes exactly. That was a 5s burst of 3k rps. The runtime auto-queued short lived requests to spare the long-running session pinned to GPU. You can see fallback routing to dedicated-style instances for the burst.
[06:45] Markus: fallback routing — does it require different model artifacts? We have quantized variants for cost.
[06:54] Owen: we route to compatible model variants; if a model isn't available with the same quantization we can fallback to a higher-latency but compatible option, or queue. The console shows the route change and the degrade policy.
[07:10] [08:00] Lena: can we talk about timeouts? Our frontends have 30s socket timeouts. If the first tokens are delayed due to a heavy pinned session, customers see errors.
[08:20] Owen: two engineering levers: (1) quick handshake tokens — an initial few tokens synthesized from a cache to satisfy the client while the full generation warms up, (2) pre-warming a lightweight responder for 1-2 tokens that are cheap but signals progress. Both reduce observed client 30s timeouts.
[08:40] Sofia: that sounds like a partial response hack — any effect on model outputs? We can't send garbage first tokens.
[08:49] Owen: it's not garbage, it's cached context-based prefix tokens derived from the session. If none exist we won't fake. It's a progressive approach — real prefix tokens.
[09:05] [10:00] Rajiv: What about tail latency during compaction or GC on the host? We've seen pauses when memory compaction runs.
[10:15] Owen: Redwood avoids host-level GC pauses by isolating GPU memory management, plus we do staggered background compactions during low SLO periods. Console signals a maintenance window; you can configure deferral to non-business hours.
[10:30] Markus: can you expose the GC triggers? We need to audit them.
[10:36] Owen: yes, audit logs include memory pressure events; they appear in our tracing and you can export to your SIEM.
[10:44] [12:00] Lena: shoutout for security questions — Rajiv asked about VPC and KMS — we do private control plane options. For KMS you can bring your key (BYOK) via standard KMS integrations or HSM for on-prem.
[12:20] Rajiv: good, that's non-negotiable. Also need SOC2 compliance and per-token audit logging.
[12:30] Lena: we have SOC2 and provide per-request audit logs and retention controls as part of the enterprise package. We'll send the security checklist after the call.
[12:45] Hannah: procurement question — pricing for the dedicated fallback + burst?
[12:53] Lena: two parts: reserved capacity for pinned sessions and on-demand burst at a premium. We'll send a pricing matrix.
[13:05] [15:00] Owen: resuming the demo — now I'm going to throttle the client read speed to emulate backpressure. Watch the worker queue length increase in the console.
[15:20] [15:45] CONSOLE: worker queue goes from 2 to 18; streaming window saturates; runtime starts shedding best-effort requests.
[15:50] Sofia: so the shedding is transparent? Do we return 429s? Or do you queue and delay?
[15:58] Owen: configurable: either immediate 429, queue with soft timeouts, or apply degraded routing to a cheaper model. For production we'd set policy per-route and per-tenant.
[16:10] Rajiv: show us the per-tenant limits in the console.
[16:22] [17:00] Owen: here — per-tenant view. You can set streaming concurrency, token rate caps, and burst windows. You can also pin specific sessions to GPU pools in Dedicated.
[17:30] Markus: about pinning — what's the eviction policy if we need to reclaim for emergency bursts?
[17:40] Owen: we do preemptive eviction with a TTL and a graceful fallback policy: re-route or checkpoint session state to KV cold storage. That can add a small resumed-latency hit but keeps system healthy.
[18:05] [20:00] Tara: quick product note on Optimize — we'll propose quantization profiles by workload segment: long-history sessions get aggressive KV caching + medium quantization, short sessions use low-latency quantization. We can attach expected cost deltas in the optimize report.
[20:25] Sofia: what about eval/regression monitoring? We need alerts if quality degrades after quantization.
[20:34] Tara: Optimize ties quality monitors to prompt sets and will trigger regression alerts when chosen metrics move beyond thresholds. We can run automated A/B with canary rollouts.
[20:50] [22:00] Rajiv: can we demo a canary rollback in the console?
[22:10] Owen: sure — I'm launching a canary with reduced traffic and a 5% sample. You can watch the routing and the automatic rollback if latency or error budget is violated. (typing) Rolling out... and rollback triggered — console shows it flipped back after 90s due to error spikes.
[22:40] Markus: nice. How do you calculate the error budget? Is it token-based or request-based?
[22:48] Owen: configurable — you can use p99 latency, error-rate, or a composite score. We support SLA-based budgets tied to tokens/sec as well.
[23:05] [25:00] Hannah: we still have procurement constraints: need a pilot contract with liability limits and specified data residency for EU customers.
[25:20] Lena: we'll include EU data residency options in the pilot addendum and push the legal review forward.
[25:35] Rajiv: we wanted to ask about SDKs for streaming clients. Do you support resumable streams? Our web clients sometimes drop and need to resume mid-generation.
[25:50] Owen: yes, resumable streams are supported via a session cursor and KV checkpointing. The SDKs include a small handshake to request resumed offset. Note some models with internal state require consistent determinism for exact resumption; we document that in the SDK.
[26:20] Sofia: is there a size limit for the session cursor? We have sessions with many embedded artifacts (images + text).
[26:30] Owen: session metadata is stored in KV; we recommend storing large artifacts externally and passing pointers. The KV is for token histories and small metadata.
[26:45] [28:00] CONVERSATION: small cross talk — "does this affect billing?" "yes tokens for replays".
[28:30] Owen: I'm going to inject a long GC event to show pause behavior — you might see a brief spike in p999.
[28:50] [29:30] CONSOLE: p999 spikes to 1.2s briefly, background compaction completes, system recovers.
[29:45] Rajiv: okay that's within tolerable limits. What about long-term KV growth? Do you have auto-compaction policies?
[29:55] Owen: yes TTL policies, bloom filters for evictions, and compaction windows. You can configure auto-trim based on token age or session activity.
[30:10] [31:00] Tara: one more Optimize demo — cost estimates for different routing policies. I'm uploading a baseline using the sample distribution you provided in advance. (note: sample distribution was synthetic) If you share real traces, numbers will change but this should show relative gains.
[31:30] Sofia: looks useful. We'll feed traces after the call.
[31:40] [33:00] Rajiv: can you talk about network egress and cross-region penalties? We have EU customers served from US today.
[33:12] Lena: you can pin workloads to regions; cross-region fallback adds latency and egress costs. We'll map costs in the pricing matrix.
[33:30] Markus: and for private deployments, what's the control plane model?
[33:38] Lena: you can run a private control plane in your VPC; compute nodes can be in your cloud account or in Redwood-managed clusters. Audit logs ship to your S3 or SIEM.
[33:52] [35:00] Sofia: are there examples of other customers running multi-hour contexts? Curious reference points.
[35:08] Owen: yes, a few fintech and legal search customers run extended sessions. We can share anonymized case notes.
[35:20] Lena: ok time to summarize and agree next steps. From Redwood: we'll send the tailored benchmark plan, SOC2 + KMS checklist, and a pricing + pilot contract. From Opal: you'll share traces and confirm pilot approver.
[35:40] Rajiv: timeline — we want a pilot in early September. If results look good we'll expand to Dedicated.
[35:52] Lena: sounds good — Owen, any final tech notes?
[36:00] Owen: just one more demo: I'm going to intentionally drop TCP reads to show how the runtime fails fast and surfaces an actionable log.
[36:12] [37:00] CONSOLE: failure logged: stream read timeout, connection recycled for that worker, session checkpointed.
[37:20] Sofia: can you share the log format? Our SIEM requires JSON with specific fields.
[37:28] Owen: yes the logs are JSON; we'll attach an example.
[37:40] [40:00] Short cross talk about canary windows and compliance.
[40:30] Hannah: procurement — can we get an itemized list for legal? We need indemnity language and subprocessor list.
[40:40] Lena: we'll include those in the legal packet.
[41:00] [42:00] Rajiv: last deep question: in fully private on-prem, do you still do smart routing or is it a single control plane?
[42:12] Owen: in private deployments you can choose: a private control plane with Redwood's routing logic or a stripped-down control plane if you want to fully own scheduling. Most pick the private control plane to keep features like fallbacks and Optimize.
[42:30] Markus: any differences in SLA/uptime if we self-host compute?
[42:38] Lena: yes self-hosted compute moves some operational responsibility to you; Redwood's SLA covers the control plane in the enterprise package or you can opt for managed compute with SLA.
[42:52] [45:00] Closing: recap of next steps and action items.
[45:20] Lena: Thanks everyone. We'll email the materials and schedule the pilot kickoff.
[45:30] Rajiv: thanks all, appreciate the detail.
[45:36] Owen: thanks, looking forward.
[46:00] End of call.

Notes on transcription quality: there are a few mis-heard acronyms (VPC sometimes transcribed as V.P.C., KV cache sometimes K.V.), occasional dropped words during shared screen audio.
notes: Demo emphasized progressive streaming mitigation (initial handshake tokens), KV/prefix caching, routing to compatible model variants for bursts, and console-based canary + rollback. Security requirements (BYOK KMS, SOC2, audit logs) noted. Pilot agreed for early September.
